title: PM chairs valedictory session of National Departmental Summit on Women and Child Development
subtitle:
Emphasising Jan Bhagidari, PM calls for making Anganwadis as Centres of community participation

PM suggests Universities could adopt nearby Anganwadi Centres and undertake social-impact studies

On women’s safety, PM emphasises on preventive actions through convergence of efforts across various departments

PM calls for greater focus on the health, nutrition and overall development of adolescent girls
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                09 OCT 2026 9:41PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi chaired the valedictory session of the two-day National Departmental Summit on Women and Child Development, at Sushma Swaraj Bhawan earlier today.
The Summit, part of the series of Departmental Summits envisioned by the Prime Minister, brought together Ministers and senior officials from States and Union Territories for focused deliberations on nutrition and early childhood care, child protection, women’s safety and empowerment, and strengthening delivery of services through greater convergence.
Prime Minister appreciated the intensive deliberations and emphasised the importance of collaborative decision-making between the Centre and States. He suggested that States could take this model further by organising similar Chintan Shivirs at the district level and at Nagar Palika and Mahanagar Palika levels. He also suggested dedicated Chintan Shivirs for Anganwadi Workers to enable them to exchange experiences, innovations and practical solutions from the field.
Emphasising Jan Bhagidari, Prime Minister stressed that an Anganwadi Centre should not function as an isolated institution but become a centre of community participation. He said families living around Anganwadi Centres could also be encouraged to contribute on special occasions by sharing nutritious food, toys and locally relevant items for children.
Prime Minister called for deeper engagement of universities and educational institutions with Anganwadi Centres. Universities could adopt nearby Anganwadi Centres and undertake social-impact studies, creating opportunities for students to contribute while also generating useful insights for improving service delivery. Medical students and NSS and NCC volunteers could similarly be associated with Anganwadi Centres and community initiatives, he said. He also called for greater focus on the health, nutrition and overall development of adolescent girls.
Prime Minister discussed issues concerning women’s safety, he suggested developing age-appropriate modules for children on women’s safety, dignity and empowerment. He also laid emphasis on preventive actions through convergence of efforts across various departments.
Highlighting the close relationship between cleanliness, health and nutrition, Prime Minister called upon Women and Child Development Departments across the country to take active ownership of the Swachhata Abhiyan. He stressed that good health and nutrition begin with cleanliness and that Anganwadi Centres and surrounding communities could become important platforms for promoting this behavioural change.
Prime Minister observed that national movements such as Vocal for Local and One District One Product (ODOP) should be promoted for Women Empowerment. He added that women’s collectives and community institutions could become important partners in strengthening local products, livelihoods and economic empowerment.
Prime Minister emphasised that the Ministry of Women and Child Development and its counterparts in the States are entrusted with responsibilities touching one of the largest and most important segments of society. The children being nurtured in Anganwadi Centres today will become the youth and citizens who build Viksit Bharat.

title: PM interacts with Team India representatives at 48th WorldSkills Competition
subtitle:
Emphasising the importance of Skill training institutions, PM says they are no less than IITs and IIMs

PM suggests that as technology evolves, young people must continuously acquire new skills and upgrade their existing capabilities

PM emphasises the need for coordinated efforts to establish India as a global hub of skilled human resources

Participants share their experiences of adapting to new tools, software, technical systems and work processes
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                09 OCT 2026 4:45PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi interacted with the representatives of Team India at WorldSkills Competition, Shanghai 2026 at 7, Lok Kalyan Marg, earlier today.
During the interaction, the participants shared their experiences during the competition. They expressed pride in representing their country at the world stage. The participants discussed adapting to new tools, software, technical systems and work processes during the international competition. They also spoke about the work being done by the government towards skill development which is helping youth.
Prime Minister congratulated the participants for representing India on the global stage. He urged them to become ambassadors of skill development. He said that practical skills are as important as academic degrees.
Highlighting the importance of specialised skills, Prime Minister said as technology evolves rapidly, young people must continuously acquire new skills, upgrade their existing capabilities and adapt to emerging technologies. He urged the participants to develop skills in line with the requirements of the international market and contribute to improving India's skill training ecosystem through their experiences and suggestions. He emphasised the need for coordinated efforts by youth, the Government and training institutions to establish India as a global hub of skilled human resources.
Prime Minister underlined the objective behind establishing a separate Ministry for Skill Development and said that the importance of skill training institutions is no less than IITs and IIMs. He encouraged the participants to share their experiences and suggestions with the Government to help improve India's skill training system.
WorldSkills is the world's leading international skills competition, bringing together young professionals from participating countries and regions to demonstrate excellence across a wide range of vocational and technical skills. WorldSkills Shanghai 2026, the 48th WorldSkills Competition, was held from 22 to 27 September 2026 at the National Exhibition and Convention Center in Shanghai. Team India secured 10th position at the 48th WorldSkills Competition, Shanghai 2026, winning 6 Silver Medals and 20 Medals for Excellence. India was represented by its largest-ever contingent of 70 competitors participating across 63 skills.
The interaction was also attended by Shri Jayant Chaudhary, Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Skill Development and Entrepreneurship and the Minister of State for Education and senior officials of Government of India.

title: PRESS RELEASE ON the 382nd  REPORT OF The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Education, Women, Children, Youth and Sports on "Reforms and Strengthening of the National Testing Agency (NTA)"
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                09 OCT 2026 5:33PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Education, Women, Children, Youth and Sports headed by Shri Mukul Wasnik, M.P., Rajya Sabha presented the 382nd Report on "Reforms and Strengthening of the National
Testing Agency (NTA)" pertaining to the Department of Higher Education, Ministry of Education to the Hon’ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha on 9th October, 2026.
2.         The Committee during the course of preparation of the 382nd Report, heard the views of Secretary, Department of Higher Education, Ministry of Education; Secretary, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare; Chairperson, National Testing Agency; Director General, National Testing Agency; Dr. K. Radhakrishnan, Former Secretary, Department of Space & Chairman, High-Level Committee of Experts and other representatives of the Department, and examined the subject in detail.
3.         The Report was considered and adopted by the Committee at its meeting held on 25th August, 2026. The Observations/Recommendations made by the Committee in the Report are enclosed herewith.
4.         The Report is also available on the following link:-
https://sansad.in/rs/committees/16?departmentally-related-standing-committees
382nd Report
OBSERVATIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
10.1 The Committee notes that under the National Education Policy 2020, the National Testing Agency has been vested with very important responsibilities. It conducts all of India’s most significant public examinations such as JEE-Mains, NEET-UG, UGC-NET, and CUET, among others and therefore acts as the gateway for the higher education system. In total, the NTA conducts examinations for which about 1.2 crore students sit annually. Moreover, the successful conduct of an all India exam like NEET requires a whole-of-government mobilization across departments at the Union, State, and local government level. Thus, the NTA has extremely significant responsibilities and also faces the task of coordination with multiple stakeholders.
The NTA is in a continually evolving state and its organizing structure may be finalized such that the resources and accountability structures of the NTA are in correspondence with the responsibilities which it has been vested with. In doing so, the Department may introduce appropriate Parliamentary framework that ensures NTA’s accountability to Parliament.
10.2 The Committee notes that investment in question banks is the most viable defense against paper leaks in the long-run. The repeated use of the same question sets or the practice of having examiners set new question papers every year can be a risk to the integrity of the examination process. The Committee, therefore, is of the view that NTA should invest in building a large, diverse, and continuously updated question bank which can be drawn on to set papers without the advance knowledge of the question-setters. The Committee notes that in the CBT format, question papers no longer have to be printed and transported to examination centers. Therefore, there is no compulsion to set question papers long in advance. Accordingly, the final question papers should be set very close to the examination, with questions drawn from the question bank using digital tools and only vetted by experts. Finally, the Committee emphasizes strict quarantine and sequestering of the final paper-vetters until the conclusion of the examination.
The Committee further recommends that the NTA must rely on bona fide experts from our most renowned educational institutions – including IITs, AIIMSs, IIMs, etc. - to develop its question banks and for translation. The NTA must also develop a system to check the track record of said experts to establish their integrity and to rule out any conflict of interest (e.g., owners or faculty of private coaching centers, family members giving the exam, etc.) before recruiting them.
10.3 The institutional culture matters as much as the procedures. The Committee, therefore, is of the view that National Testing Agency needs to cultivate a culture where every official from the Director General to the centre invigilator sees themselves as a guardian of examination integrity, not just as a jobholder in an administrative system.
The Committee notes that recent challenges have affected the public trust in the National Testing Agency, and that rebuilding this trust will require consistent, transparent, and two-way communication with stakeholders. The Committee notes that the NTA's present engagement with candidates is largely confined to one-way communication through portals and notifications. It notes that the NTA’s channels for feedback from students and educational institutions need greater public awareness. The Committee recommends that such channels be built into the ordinary functioning of the NTA and be widely dispersed across students, parents, and instructors, so as to enable the agency to be more responsive to stakeholder concerns.
10.4 The Committee notes the measures taken by National Testing Agency since 2024. The institutional framework including SLCCs, DLCCs, Biometric authentication, mobile jammers, AI-based CCTV analysis is welcome. However, the cancellation of NEET (UG) 2026 despite all these measures shows the need for greater procedural and institutional reforms.
10.5 The Committee notes that of the 39 sanctioned positions in the NTA, only 23 officers are currently in position and on deputation to the NTA – a vacancy of 41%. The Committee notes that the hiring of manpower to strengthen the NTA was among the key recommendations of the High-Level Expert Committee chaired by Dr. K Radhakrishnan. The Committee notes
the shortage of manpower in the NTA and
urges the agency to expedite the recruitment to all sanctioned positions.
The Committee notes that all the 39 permanent posts that exist in the NTA are currently filled through a deputation mode. Officers on deputation generally serve for a limited tenure of two to three years before returning to their parent cadres. However, the conduct of national-level entrance examinations requires considerably expertise which is generally built over several years of experience. Accordingly, a dedicated cadre of professional staff is required for this purpose. The Committee recommends that the NTA should therefore hire its own officers on a permanent basis, with a particular emphasis on specialists in psychometrics, examination security, digital infrastructure, data analytics, and examination logistics. The 16 posts under the Central Staffing Scheme should be treated as a supplementary layer of senior leadership, not as a substitute for domain expertise.
10.6 The Committee observes that for CBT examinations conducted by NTA a concrete implementation plan for secure government CBT centers, including budgetary provisioning and a current mapping of existing government-owned facilities, needs to be finalized expeditiously. The Committee is of the view that adequate government-owned infrastructure must be in place so that reliance on private centers is avoided.
10.7 The Committee notes the recommendations made by the High-Level Committee of Experts (HLCE) for a phased transition to CBT mode, and broadly concurs with this approach. The Committee notes that most entrance examinations conducted by the NTA are already run on Computer-Based-Testing, including the JEE-Mains, UGC-NET, and CUET. The Committee notes that digital literacy constitutes a critically important academic and professional skill that is increasingly prevalent among the student population. The Committee notes that the NEET-UG is an outlier in its reliance on pen-and-paper testing. The Committee therefore recommends that NEET should also be moved to a CBT approach.
The Committee however continues to have concerns about the accessibility of CBT to students from remote regions and from marginalized backgrounds. Therefore, the Committee recommends that the transition to CBT be accompanied by a concerted national testing strategy to maximize digital accessibility. Some features of the strategy may be as follows:
For NEET (UG), any transition to CBT must be preceded by significant investment in government-owned CBT infrastructure across the country, particularly in Tier-2, Tier-3 cities and rural areas. The HLCE's recommendation of 1,000 secure government CBT centers must be implemented with a clear and phased timeline to facilitate the examinations. The Committee suggests that the NTA itself to financially support the establishment of mid-sized IT labs (100-200 nodes) in schools and colleges across the country. As long as the school/college administration provide the space for the IT lab, the NTA can invest in the hardware equipment needed on the condition that the facilities be given up to the NTA for the conduct of any examination required.
The Committee emphasizes that there must be at least 1 test center in each district to offer all exams to minimize the stress and financial burden of transport and accommodation on students.
The Committee notes that private institutions engaged as examination centres on a sub-contracted basis have often proved to be a weak link in examination security. Therefore,
all centers must be owned and operated by the Union and/or State Governments.
Students must also be offered opportunities to give CBT mock exams to enable them to familiarize themselves with the format and with a digital interface.
The Ministry of Education may consider including CBT-based exams at the school level as well, to build familiarity with digital testing among students.
Before rolling out the CBT mode, in places where infrastructure for CBT is inadequate due to the absence of computers and/or connectivity, the National Testing Agency should consider a hybrid model where the encrypted questions may be delivered to the exam centre directly and then printed there itself, which the Committee has been informed is feasible, until full CBT readiness is achieved.
The multi-session nature of CBT-based NEET (UG) examination would require a robust, transparent, and independently audited normalisation methodology. This normalisation methodology should be developed and explained to the public before any transition to CBT.
Switching over the NEET (UG) to CBT mode should involve consultations with the stakeholders
viz.
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, medical education regulators, students and their families.
10.8 The Committee takes note of two procedural concerns raised before it:
Invigilators completing signing and checking formalities during the course of the examination disturbs the focus of students who are already racing against time; the Committee, therefore, is of the view that a separate 15 minutes window, before or after the test, be kept exclusively for such formalities and not in between the exam duration.
Candidates arriving a few minutes late at the exam centers are mostly denied entry altogether resulting in wasting their year-long hard work over a minor delay. The Committee observes that there are some genuine reasons due to which a candidate may arrive late at the examination centre. The Committee is of the view that some mechanism be evolved such that students be allowed entry into the exam hall after signing an undertaking recording their late arrival and be allowed to attempt the exam only for the remaining time, with no extra time granted under any circumstances.
10.9 The Committee notes that public rallies, processions, or large gatherings on the day of examination can delay candidates and cause them to miss their reporting time. The Committee recommends that the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024 be amended to direct District Administration to withhold permission for any rally, procession, or any other public gathering on examination days, and to ensure that smooth traffic and law-and-order arrangements are in place well in advance, so that no candidate is affected by an avoidable, external disturbance.
10.10 The Committee notes that presently NEET (UG) qualifies far more candidates than the seats available across MBBS, BDS, AYUSH, and nursing courses put together. A reasonably wide qualifying pool gives students a fair chance through counseling rounds and private or deemed seats, but an excessively wide gap creates needless stress for lakhs of students. The Committee, therefore, is of the view that NTA and the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare should undertake a data-based, year-wise review of the qualifying percentile and cut-off methodology, keeping the number of qualified candidates reasonably aligned to actual seat availability, without compromising merit.
10.11 The Committee notes that, contrary to the Civil Services Examination that follows a multi-stage format for filtration of candidates, NEET (UG) examination remains a single-stage test that covers MBBS, BDS, nursing, and AYUSH admissions together handling more than 22 lakh students. The Committee is of the view that NTA should examine the feasibility of a two-stage format for its large examinations, such as having a common prelims examination for all medical streams while conducting specialized mains stage for specific courses, so that a candidate seeking nursing or AYUSH is tested and ranked apart from one seeking admission to MBBS, reducing avoidable competition.
10.12 The Committee notes that firms involved in examination-related services such as paper setting, logistics, printing, administration etc. that have been blacklisted by one or more State government(s) or organisation(s) have continued to secure contracts with other States and organisations. There is currently no preventive mechanism to counter this malpractice.
The Committee recommends that NTA should create and maintain a National Registry of Blacklisted Examination Vendors. This registry should include the names of firms, their associated individuals and entities, the nature of the disqualification, and the authority that imposed it. It should be publicly accessible online. Contracting with any entity on this list by NTA, any State Government(s), or any other public examination authority should be considered under the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024. The Committee notes that it has previously made the same recommendation in its 371st report on the Autonomous Bodies of the Higher Education Department.
10.13 The Committee notes that the coaching industry has effectively created a parallel curriculum that often matters more than the official school curriculum. It is a direct consequence of examination design choices. When examination papers tests beyond the NCERT or state board syllabus, or test rapid recall and pattern-recognition developed through repetitive practice rather than genuine conceptual understanding, they inevitably reward coaching over learning. This design has fostered a large, largely unregulated private coaching industry that displaced school-level learning as the primary site of preparation for these examinations. Moreover, it creates a barrier to socio-economic mobility by privileging students who can afford coaching have a structural advantage over equally talented students who cannot.
The Committee is of the view that the Ministry of Education should ensure that there should be specific, measurable standards for ensuring that NEET (UG), JEE (Main), and CUET papers test conceptual understanding based on the official school curriculum, rather than rewarding techniques specific to coaching. Further, there should be a regulatory framework for the coaching industry, with attention to fee transparency, safety standards, and the mental health of students in coaching centers.
10.14 The Committee was informed, during the course of its meetings, that the NTA only has data on the number of candidates registered from different States for various examinations and no data on whether those students succeeded or not. Participation data and success data are very different things. A State may have high registration numbers but poor pass rates, pointing to a quality or access problem.
The Committee recommends that NTA should conduct an annual Equity Audit examining, for each major examination, the participation rates, pass rates, and cutoff achievement rates of candidates disaggregated by State, gender, school board type (government, aided, private), medium of instruction, and social category (OBC, SC, ST, EWS, general). The audit findings should be published in NTA's Annual Report and submitted to the Ministry of Education for policy consideration. The Ministry of Education may utilise the data for policy consideration.
10.15 The Committee notes that the intense pressure of a single high-stakes examination affects the mental health of lakhs of young candidates, before, during, and after the declaration of results. The Committee is of the view that NTA partners with mental health prof1essionals to offer free, accessible counseling helplines, circulate simple stress-management material well ahead of each examination, and ensure that examination centers maintain a calm, supportive environment, particularly during the sensitive period surrounding results.
10.16 During the course of its meetings, the Committee was apprised that presently NEET (UG) has no limit on how many times a candidate can attempt it, and no real upper age limit either. This has resulted in anomalies such as the participation of candidates above the age of 70 years in the NEET examinations. The Committee recommends that the Ministry explore, alongside the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare and all other relevant stakeholders, possibilities of reasonable age limits and reasonable attempt limits to all major examinations including the NEET-UG. The Committee notes that an exception to this rule may be made only for the UGC-NET.
10.17 The Committee notes that the cooperation and expertise of the State Governments is critical to the success of the examinations. Therefore, it recommends that a revamped NTA must include adequate representation from State Governments on its Governing Body.
The Committee recommends that the NTA must be reimagined not just as a body to administer exams but as a think-tank for all matters and policies relating to examinations. The NTA must have a research wing staffed by academics with credentials in education research other than bureaucrats and officers. The absence of a research wing currently precludes the NTA from conducting critical tasks like longitudinal studies that gauge if the NEET, CUET, UGC-NET exams etc. actually fulfill their intended purpose.  Similarly, a NTA with deep academic expertise can also be a resource for other educational institutions like the CBSE which are implementing interventions like the introduction of an OnScreen Marking system in Board Examinations. The Committee thus recommends greater academic and research expertise in the NTA to help it better conduct its own examinations as well as eventually to facilitate non-NTA examinations.
The Committee notes that once the NTA's digital infrastructure has matured, examinations should be conducted on CBT basis with a Computer Adaptive Testing (CAT) model which is universally regarded as the gold standard for assessment. This will require the use of AI tools that can pull questions from a large question bank, modify them to the aptitude of the student, evaluate questions correctly, and normalize scores based on objective considerations such as the difficulty of the questions. Such a system will minimize the scope for malpractices. There will be no standard question paper that can be leaked. Further, no two candidates at the same center will receive an identical set of questions, reducing the scope for cheating. Accordingly, the NTA should set up a technical team with the proficiency to develop, monitor, and continuously strengthen these tools.
The Committee was informed by the NTA that the risk of a CBT examination would be that the computer system is vulnerable to hacking by malicious agents and that such hacks are also hard to track. The Committee was informed that such an attempt occurred and was investigated by the CBI during the IIT JEE-Mains Examination of 2021. The Committee notes that the transition to CBT therefore presents new challenges which the NTA must anticipate and be prepared for. In addition to live CCTV monitoring, the Committee recommends the establishment of a robust, in-house cybersecurity team within the NTA which can develop and implement
secure examination software that prevents remote access, screen-recording, and the use of virtual machines. Further it must adopt AI-based analytical tools to detect and flag anomalous response patterns that may indicate malpractice.
The Committee notes that the Director General is the key executive officer in the NTA. However, between 23.06.2024 and 01.04.2026, the position was held as an additional charge by officers who had substantial primary responsibilities as CMD, ITPO and Commissioner, NVS. The Committee discourages the practice of appointing officers to key positions in the NTA as an additional charge.
While the number of sanctioned posts has increased since 2024, the Committee notes that even at full strength of 39 officers, the NTA will have to rely on third-party private contractors. The Committee recommends that the NTA must eventually grow its operations to be able to conduct the logistics of all examinations by itself. The use of non-NTA employees must be limited to the setting of papers and other academic functions for which reliance on outside academic expertise is critical.
The Committee notes that the NTA has a substantial annual revenue surplus, and in total has acquired a total revenue surplus of Rs. 590 crores between FY 2018-2019 and FY 2024-2025. The Committee was informed that the surplus funds available with NTA from time to time are being invested in Fixed Deposits for optimal utilization until they are required for operational purposes. The Committee notes that this corpus can be used for investment and upgradation in government-owned CBT centers and the conduct of the mock examinations to familiarize students with the CBT interface.
The Committee notes that the NEET-UG results are generally not published in a publicly accessible manner.
However, in 2024, the NTA published the details on the instance of the Honourable Supreme Court and it sparked a larger public conversation on how student performance across cities and test centers varies. Consequently, the NTA cracked down on the ability of students to choose their own test centers. The Committee has noted that this is a progressive measure which has reduced scope for misuse.
Accordingly, the Committee recommends that the NTA should follow the practices adopted by the UPSC of transparency in results. The Committee notes that such transparency can enable the NTA to identify any anomalous patterns in the performance of candidates and test centers and enhance the public trust in the NEET examination.
The Committee envisions that the NTA should have in-house capabilities that can detect, trace, and determine prima facie irregularities in the examination system. Such in-house capabilities can strengthen the NTA’s ability to rapidly respond to crises. Accordingly, the Committee recommends that the Ministry consider building some of these abilities within the NTA.
The Committee notes that there is presently no official public record of paper leaks, the FIRs registered on paper leaks, and how these cases are being investigated and prosecuted by the CBI and other investigative agencies. The Department of Higher Education stated to the Committee that although examination malpractices/disruptions have occurred, no paper leak has occurred in an exam conducted by the NTA since its formation in 2017 till 2025. The Committee noted that the Ministry’s assertion is at variance with the opinion of some Members of the Committee. Accordingly, the Committee recommends that the NTA work with the Department of Higher Education and other Government agencies and departments to issue a publicly-available report documenting all relevant details relating to the exams that have been conducted by the NTA and any investigations pertaining to them.
The Committee notes that the Expert Committee chaired by Dr. K Radhakrishnan had recommended that the NTA's mandate be confined to the conduct of entrance examinations, with the NTA taking on additional functions only after demonstrating expanded institutional capacity. The Committee notes that the NTA continues to conduct recruitment examinations that are not connected to admission into higher education institutions. The Committee recommends that the NTA immediately refocus its priorities to the conduct of admission tests to higher education institutions alone. The Committee notes that such a refocusing would be in line with the NTA’s mission statement – “[T]o improve equity and quality in education by administering research based valid, reliable, efficient, transparent, fair and international level assessments.”
The Committee recommends that the NTA should bring out a clear duty of care owed by it to candidates. It may include the provision of financial compensation for candidates affected by administrative cancellations and prescribe timelines for grievance redressal. This will reduce the financial and psychological burden that such events place on candidates.
The Committee also recommends a secure channel for receipt of information and grievance redressal related to all aspects of examination.
The Committee recommends the creation of an independent mechanism for Educational Examinations, functioning independently of the NTA, with powers to audit examination security protocols, investigate candidate grievances, and submit its report directly to the Ministry.
The Committee recommends that the NTA invest in the training and capacity-building of all relevant stakeholders – including those from State Governments and other agencies – who are actually responsible for the conduct of examinations at the district and test center-level, so that reforms are internalised rather than merely complied with
.
10.32 The Committee notes that the implementation of the Dr. Radhakrishnan Committee’s 101 recommendations to strengthen the examination process is ongoing. The Committee was informed that the majority of reforms have been implemented, since 60 of the 101 recommendations pertained to the year 2025 and 2026. The Committee recommends the expedited implementation of the pending reforms, including for any of the 60 reforms relating to 2025 and 2026 that are yet to be implemented.
10.33 The Committee recommends that the NTA also develop a protocol for exam administration for students with disabilities who have distinct requirements and needs. The NTA should strengthen support for students with disabilities by ensuring accessible examination centres, the possibility of adequate scribes and compensatory time, accessible digital platforms, and a dedicated grievance-redressal mechanism. Such a provision can help enhance the accessibility of higher education to students.
10.34 The Committee recommends that to the extent that any printing is required post the transition to CBT-exams, it should be conducted only in NTA-owned and operated printing presses. There must be no reliance on private printers for the same.
10.35 The Committee recognizes that education remains a fundamental pillar of national progress and social development, with the potential to empower individuals and strengthen the nation’s future. The Committee believes that continued reforms in the examination system is now a national imperative, with a view to eliminating unfair means, reducing undue stress, and encouraging a more holistic assessment of students’ abilities. The Committee resolves to stay apprised of the matter and encourages all stakeholders to contribute ideas for this shared national mission of a better examination and education system.

title: Coal supply to power plants gathers pace in October
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                09 OCT 2026 10:54AM by PIB Delhi
content:
Some recent media reports flag growing risk of Power shortages in India as coal inventories at power plants fall to low levels. In this context, the Ministry of Coal would like to clarify the following.
The "critical stock" tag is a norm-based trigger (plants holding less than the prescribed threshold of normative stock) and is designed to flag plants early, well before actual fuel shortage or generation loss occurs. A plant appearing on this list is, by design, an early-warning entry and not an indication that it has run out of coal or is at imminent risk of shutting down.
Coal stock position needs to be viewed alongside the improvement since the September trough in supplies. Daily supplies to the power sector have risen by around 36% from the September low, with October averaging about 9% higher than September. The rate of stock depletion has also moderated significantly (Figure 1). Rail loading has strengthened correspondingly, averaging over 465 rakes per day in October, with the 470-rake target achieved on three consecutive days (Figure 2). Supplies through other modes, including road, have also improved.
Figure 1:
Depletion/Accretion in DCB Plants (MT)
Figure 2: Total rake loading trend, October 2026
Stock depletion has slowed sharply, with the daily drawdown falling by more than half from 0.243 MT/day in September to 0.116 MT/day in October. The position is therefore stabilising, although stock rebuilding is yet to commence.
The rise in plants with critical stocks is being closely monitored, with requirement-based redistribution of coal to vulnerable stations to ensure adequate supplies and uninterrupted power generation. With the monsoon receding and peak demand expected to moderate by mid-October (as per historical trends) sustained loading of 465–475 rakes per day should support further stabilisation and enable stock rebuilding ahead of the festive, winter and subsequent summer demand periods, thereby reducing the number of plants in the critical category.
The Ministry of Coal, in close coordination with the Ministries of Railways and Ministry of Power, is actively monitoring supplies and logistics to ensure that coal availability does not constrain power generation anywhere in the country.

title: Commerce Secretary Shri Rajesh Agrawal Highlights Need for Rigorous Legal Thinking at CTIL’s 9th Anniversary Celebration
subtitle: CTIL Releases 9th Anniversary Magazine on Trade and Sustainability, Launches Special Edition of Investment Law Compass
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                09 OCT 2026 11:33AM by PIB Delhi
content:
Commerce Secretary Shri Rajesh Agrawal, in his video address at the 9th Anniversary Celebration of Centre for Trade and Investment Law (CTIL), held at the Prime Minister’s Museum and Library in New Delhi, on 7 October 2026, said that established rules were being questioned, while emerging issues such as sustainability-linked trade measures and digital trade were reshaping the global trade agenda. He noted that rigorous legal thinking was more important than ever and that CTIL, as a leading institution in the field, was well placed to contribute to it.
Commerce Secretary Shri Rajesh Agrawal, congratulated CTIL on completing nine years and noted that the Centre had earned the trust of the Government, industry and the wider trade law community through its sustained and rigorous work. He recalled CTIL’s contributions to the Department of Commerce through legal analysis and specialised support in free trade agreement negotiations, dispute settlement and institutional memory building.
India needs institutions like CTIL that do more than follow developments in international economic law and are capable of shaping them, noted Justice P. S. Narasimha, Judge, Supreme Court of India.
Justice Narasimha observed that international investment law has evolved from an initial focus on the protection of foreign investment towards greater recognition of the regulatory freedom of States. He noted that the field is now entering a phase in which questions of institutionalisation, legitimacy and the long-term balance between investment and public power have assumed greater significance. He underscored the need for a durable international investment law framework that balances investment protection with the regulatory authority of States.
Head, CTIL, Indian Institute of Foreign Trade (IIFT), and WTO India Chair, Prof. James J. Nedumpara, highlighted that CTIL was established to strengthen India’s trade capacity as a broader element of economic statecraft. He noted that CTIL had provided more than 4,000 legal opinions, participated in negotiations concerning nearly 10 free trade agreements, and contributed to WTO negotiations, submissions, notifications and dispute settlement.
Additional Secretary, Ministry of Commerce and Industry, Shri Yashvir Singh, delivered the Special Address and highlighted CTIL’s contributions to India’s major trade engagements, including support for major free trade agreements and engagements such as the G20 and BRICS over the past several years. He also highlighted CTIL’s work in WTO negotiations, notifications and dispute settlement, along with its contributions to India’s economic diplomacy and the development of human capital in international economic law.
Vice Chancellor, IIFT, Dr. K. Rangarajan, in his address, recalled the evolution of specialised trade-policy institutions at IIFT. He highlighted CTIL’s growing role in providing timely expertise for international trade negotiations and policy interventions.
Joint Secretary, Ministry of Commerce and Industry, Smt. Kapil Chaudhary, highlighted CTIL’s expanding research in emerging areas, including critical minerals, semiconductors, artificial intelligence, supply chains, climate and sustainability. She also emphasised the need for institutional knowledge management and greater capacity building within the Department of Commerce.
On the occasion, the ninth anniversary issue of the CTIL Magazine, titled “The Emerging Sustainability Landscape: Responding to Shifting Winds”, was released. The magazine examines the future opportunities and challenges that developing countries may face as they seek to participate in the evolving intersection of trade and sustainability. A special anniversary edition of Investment Law Compass, CTIL’s monthly newsletter on developments in investment law and policy, was also launched.
The formal proceedings concluded with the presentation of Distinguished Long Service Awards to members of the CTIL faculty and staff.

content:
The 3rd International Bharat 6G Symposium 2026 concluded at Yashobhoomi, Dwarka, New Delhi, with a valedictory address by Dr. Chandra Sekhar Pemmasani, Union Minister of State for Communications and Rural Development. Organised by the Bharat 6G Alliance (B6GA) alongside India Mobile Congress 2026, the three-day event brought together global telecom leaders, policymakers, standards organisations, industry, academia and researchers to discuss the roadmap towards IMT-2030 and beyond.
Union Minister of State for Communications and Rural Development is his address congratulated the Bharat 6G Alliance for organizing the two-day 3rd International Bharat 6G Symposium 2026 and for inviting over 75 speakers, which included more than 30 international experts.
The Union Minister of State said that India is moving from being one of the world’s largest telecom markets to becoming an important telecom technology nation and our indigenous technology journey has taught us something important: Self-reliance and global collaboration are not opposites. The stronger our capabilities, the stronger the partner we can be to the world. The Union Minister of State highlighted that 6G must not create a new digital divide while we are still closing the old one. Affordability, accessibility and coverage must therefore be design requirements — not afterthoughts and in 6G, connectivity need not end where the tower ends. The integration of terrestrial and satellite networks can take connectivity further — to remote villages, islands, oceans and places that traditional networks struggle to reach. India is ready to test these technologies at scale — and share what we learn with the world. Our national goal is Viksit Bharat — a developed India by 2047, the hundredth year of our independence.
The experts contributed to sessions on 5G-Advanced foundations for 6G, global standards, spectrum and WRC-27, international trials and testbeds, AI-native and sustainable networks, startups and academia, global alliances, and industrial use cases. The Symposium emphasized that global interoperability and inclusive 6G development will depend on collaboration across countries, industry, research institutions and standards bodies.
The Symposium reaffirmed India’s commitment to contributing to global 6G research and standards while building indigenous capabilities and strengthening international partnerships. Its discussions called for coordinated standards development, collaborative research, spectrum harmonization and large-scale testing, with affordability, accessibility, security and sustainability embedded in the design of future networks.
A key outcome was the exchange of five new MoUs with GSMA, one6G, GTI Alliance, 6G Innovation Forum (6G IF) Taiwan and VOICE, strengthening opportunities for international cooperation, joint research, trials and knowledge exchange. B6GA also released ten white papers and reports, including a Progress Report on 6G Joint Principles, reflecting continued work towards a 6G ecosystem that is secure, open, resilient, inclusive and sustainable by design.
During the valedictory session in the presence of the Minister of State for Communications, the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) presented a curtain raiser for the Emerging Science, Technology and Innovation Conclave (ESTIC) 2026. The second edition of this national science and technology platform is scheduled from 27–29 October 2026 at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi, under the guidance of the Office of the Principal Scientific Adviser and organised by CSIR in collaboration with 12 participating departments/Ministries. Its theme is “Creative Minds, Catalyzing Science, Empowering Technologies”.
The three-day Conclave features plenary talks, 9 thematic technical sessions, panel discussions, presentations by science and technology leaders and deep-tech Startups, exhibitions and B2B/B2G connect meetings.
In the 2nd edition of ESTIC 2026 , DoT is identified to led the  thematic session “Intelligent Networks and Quantum Communication”, scheduled for 28 October 2026. The session will explore technologies shaping future digital infrastructure and secure communications. It will feature a keynote by Mr. N. G. The workshop reaffirmed the Government’s focus on fostering collaboration among academia, industry and research institutions to accelerate technology development, promote indigenous solutions and prepare India’s talent pool for the 5G Advanced and 6G era.
By placing young innovators and academic research at the centre of technological advancement, the initiative supports India’s ambition to emerge as a global hub for telecommunications innovation and contribute to the vision of a technologically empowered and self-reliant nation.

Building Intelligent Networks for Viksit Bharat 2047

title: Union Minister of Communications Shri Jyotiraditya M. Scindia Holds Media Interaction at India Mobile Congress 2026; Calls for Taking Indian Technologies to the World
subtitle:
“The next decade is not to bring the world to India but to take India to the world”: Union Minister Shri Scindia

Union Minister of Communications emphasizes India’s Shift from Digital Connectivity to Global Telecom Technology Leadership at Media Interaction
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                09 OCT 2026 7:02PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Union Minister for Communications and Development of North Eastern Region Shri Jyotiraditya M. Scindia held a media interaction on the 10th edition of India Mobile Congress (IMC) 2026 highlighting India’s transformation from expanding digital connectivity to developing indigenous technologies and strengthening its position in the global telecommunications ecosystem. The Union Minister emphasised that the next phase of India’s telecom journey would focus on designing, developing and manufacturing technologies in India for domestic and international markets, with closer collaboration between the Government and industry.
Reflecting on the journey of the past decade, the Union Minister said that while the last decade was marked by the expansion of digital connectivity, the next decade must focus on building indigenous technological capabilities, accelerating the deployment of innovations and expanding the global reach of Indian products.
Organised jointly by the Department of Telecommunications (DoT), Ministry of Communications, and the Cellular Operators Association of India (COAI), IMC 2026 is being held at Yashobhoomi, New Delhi under the theme “Scale Without Boundaries”. Highlighting the journey of IMC, Shri Scindia said, “IMC has become Asia’s number one digital and telecom conference at this juncture, and we hope to take it onto a global stage in the days to come.”
IMC 2026: A Global Platform for Technology and Innovation
The scale of the tenth edition is reflected in its 60,000-square-metre exhibition area, participation from over 100 countries, more than 2,000 technology use cases, over 400 startups and more than 900 thought leaders, alongside industry partners, exhibitors, investors, incubators and accelerators. Emphasising that the value of IMC extends beyond participation numbers, Union Minister Shri Scindia noted that its real impact lies in translating ideas into products, partnerships into investments and technological advances into solutions that improve citizens’ lives.
The showcased use cases demonstrate how emerging technologies are moving beyond laboratories and pilot projects into enterprises, public services and everyday applications. The platform also provides opportunities for collaboration among government, industry, academia and the startup ecosystem to accelerate the development, commercialisation and deployment of innovative solutions.
From Connectivity to Indigenous Technology Capability
Union Minister Shri Scindia said that India’s telecom transformation has advanced across three key areas: expanding connectivity, developing indigenous technological capabilities and strengthening domestic manufacturing capacity. title: Union Minister Shri Jyotiraditya M. Scindia Inaugurates AI for Good Lab Workshop at India Mobile Congress 2026
subtitle:
"The True Measure of AI Will Not Be Model Size, But the Number of Lives It Improves": Union Minister Shri Scindia

India Partners as Pilot Country with ITU to Bridge the Gap between AI Strategy and Impact Across the Global South
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                09 OCT 2026 6:17PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Union Minister for Communications and Development of North Eastern Region Shri Jyotiraditya M. Scindia inaugurated "AI for Good Lab Workshop: From Strategy to Impact," organized jointly by the Department of Telecommunications (DoT), Ministry of Communications, and the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) at the India Mobile Congress (IMC) 2026 in New Delhi. The landmark event marked a major milestone in transitioning artificial intelligence from global strategy discussions to practical deployment, local solutions, and human-centric scale. The workshop gathered key international dignitaries, including Dr. Bilel Jamoussi, Deputy Director of the ITU Telecommunication Standardization Bureau, Shri Amit Agrawal, Secretary, Department of Telecommunications along with distinguished researchers, innovators, industry leaders, and policy experts.
Addressing the gathering, the Union Minister Shri Scindia stated, “The journey of the AI for Good Lab from Geneva to New Delhi mirrors the journey that artificial intelligence itself must make—from global conversations to local solutions, from technological possibility to human impact, and from strategy to scale. The distance between AI ambition and AI impact is bridged by skills, compute, data, institutions, and connectivity. Ultimately, the true measure of artificial intelligence will not be the size of its models or the sophistication of its algorithms, but the number of human lives it improves.”
The Union Minister reiterated India's guiding philosophy of
"Sarvajan Hitaya, Sarvajan Sukhaya"
(for the welfare of all, for the happiness of all), noting that while nearly 2.2 billion people worldwide remain offline, technology must expand human opportunity rather than concentrate it, ensuring the digital divide does not morph into an AI divide.
During the address, the Minister detailed key milestones driving India's domestic AI capabilities and digital infrastructure under the ₹10,000-crore-plus IndiaAI Mission. On the compute infrastructure front, more than 38,000 high-end GPUs have been onboarded at approximately one-third of the global average cost, with an additional 20,000 GPUs being added. In terms of open data and talent, the
AI Kosh
platform is unlocking datasets and sovereign models across agriculture, healthcare, and education. India currently ranks first globally in relative AI skill penetration, with Indian developers contributing approximately 5.2% of open-source AI projects on GitHub with ten or more stars. Furthermore, telecom innovation is being paired with trust through AI and data analytics tools like
Sanchar Saathi
, which has facilitated the disconnection of over 7.14 crore fraudulent mobile connections, traced over 35 lakh lost handsets, and prevented potential financial fraud worth over ₹5,000 crore. To support standardization, India's Telecommunication Engineering Centre (TEC) has developed national standards covering AI fairness, robustness, and incident reporting, while establishing a National Working Group on AI Standardization to align with ITU-T global benchmarks.
The workshop introduced the AI for Good Lab framework, designed to help countries overcome challenges related to limited skills, fragmented innovation, and missing infrastructure through three interconnected pillars. First, the AI Readiness and Policy pillar assesses policy gaps and establishes practical governance frameworks. Second, the AI Skills Development pillar focuses on scaling national AI talent, capacity-building, and training initiatives. Third, the Public AI Infrastructure pillar establishes standards-based, interoperable AI Sandbox environments for testing, validating, scaling, and re-using locally relevant AI solutions. As one of the ten pilot countries alongside partners from Africa, Asia, Latin America, and the Gulf, India brings its model of shared compute, open datasets, and Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) to lead cross-regional learning and technical collaboration across the Global South.
The sessions delivered structured deliberation on defining a concrete roadmap for institutional engagement, priority sector adoption, and Global South knowledge-sharing. Stakeholders achieved a shared understanding of the AI Sandbox requirements to support experimentation while validating fairness, robustness, and safety before scaling solutions to the last citizen.
The workshop concluded with a summary by Dr. Bilel Jamoussi, followed by a Call for Follow-up Actions by Shri Sanjeev Kumar Sharma, Deputy Director General, AI & Digital Intelligence Unit, DoT, and special address by Shri S. T. Abbas, Sr. Deputy Director General, TEC.
The workshop reinforced the importance of sustained collaboration among Government, industry, academia, startups, civil society and international organisations to build an AI ecosystem that is innovative, inclusive, secure, trusted and beneficial for all. The discussions provided a strong foundation for moving from dialogue to implementation, from vision to action and from isolated initiatives to a collaborative movement for AI for Good and AI for All.

title: India Welcomes ITU Proposal for Joint Trials to Combat Cross-Border Telecom Fraud: Union Minister of State for Communications Dr Chandra Sekhar Pemmasani
subtitle:
Over 82 Lakh Fraudulent Mobile Connections Disconnected Through ASTR; Sanchar Saathi App Records Around 25 Million Downloads

Financial Fraud Risk Indicator helps Prevent Suspected Losses of Over ₹5,000 Crore in 15 Months

Technology, Regulation and Global Cooperation Key to Combating Fraudulent Communications: Dr Pemmasani
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                09 OCT 2026 5:32PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Union Minister of State for Communications and Rural Development, Dr Chandra Sekhar Pemmasani today, delivered the keynote address at the ITU Roundtable on “Implementing ITU Standards to Combat Fraudulent Communications.” The Roundtable was held on the sidelines of the ongoing India Mobile Congress (IMC) 2026 which was formally inaugurated by Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi on 08 October 2026, at Yashobhoomi.
Addressing the gathering, Dr Pemmasani stated that under the leadership of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi, India has connected more than a billion people, and the next task is to ensure that connectivity comes with trust. Emphasising the need for international cooperation, he stated, “Fraud is a network problem. It needs a network answer. And because networks are global, the answer must also be global.”
Highlighting the growing threat of organised, cross-border fraud, including impersonation, digital arrest scams, AI-generated voice cloning and deepfakes, Dr Pemmasani noted that Indians lost over ₹22,800 crore to such fraud in 2024. He further added that the government had learnt what works and has now built its defences in layers.
Dr Pemmasani outlined India's five-layered approach to combating fraudulent communications, including real-time blocking of spoofed international calls, identification of fraudulent mobile connections through C-DOT's AI-based ASTR tool, citizen participation through Sanchar Saathi, intelligence sharing through the Digital Intelligence Platform (DIP), and measures addressing emerging fraud channels.
The Union MoS highlighted that ASTR has helped disconnect over 82 lakh fraudulent connections, while the Sanchar Saathi app has recorded around 25 million downloads. The Digital Intelligence Platform connects over 1,600 organisations, including telecom operators, banks and law-enforcement agencies. The Financial Fraud Risk Indicator has helped prevent suspected financial losses exceeding ₹5,000 crore in 15 months.
Acknowledging the limitations of national solutions in addressing cross-border fraud, Dr Pemmasani highlighted the importance of ITU standards for digital verification of caller identity across international networks. He welcomed the ITU's proposal for joint trials involving governments, regulators, operators and technology companies, and affirmed India's readiness to contribute.
The Union MoS suggested beginning trials between willing countries on selected international routes, ensuring participation of different network technologies and incorporating lessons into the continued improvement of ITU standards. He further emphasised that as 6G networks are developed, trust must be designed in from the beginning.
Concluding his address, Dr Pemmasani emphasised that technology, regulation and collaboration must work together to combat fraudulent communications. “At home, India has moved from reaction to prevention. Now, with ITU, let us move from national solutions to global trust,” he stated.

title: TRAI releases Draft Telecommunication (Broadcasting and Cable) Services DRM-based Digital Addressable Systems Audit Manual, 2026
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:

content:
The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) has today issued the Draft Telecommunication (Broadcasting and Cable) Services Digital Rights Management (DRM) based Digital Addressable Systems Audit Manual, 2026 for seeking comments from the stakeholders.
The Telecommunication (Broadcasting and Cable) Services Interconnection (Addressable Systems) Regulations, 2017 (hereafter referred to as ‘Interconnection Regulations’) mandate annual audit of the Digital Addressable Systems (DAS) of the distributors of television channels, including CAS, SMS, DRM and other related systems, subject to the provisions of the Regulations. Schedule X of the Interconnection Regulations specifies requirements for DRM-based systems, primarily for IPTV-based distribution services.
The Telecommunication (Broadcasting and Cable) Services Digital Addressable Systems Audit Manual, 2026, issued on 10th March 2026, provides detailed clause-wise audit procedures for systems covered under Schedule III, including CAS, SMS and STB based systems. The need for a similar manual detailing audit procedures for DRM-based systems as per Schedule X of ‘Interconnection Regulations’ was highlighted by various stakeholders, including IPTV operators, broadcasters and auditors.
Accordingly, the Authority, has prepared the Draft DRM Audit Manual to provide detailed procedures for auditing compliance of DRM systems to Schedule X of the ‘Interconnection Regulations’. The Audit Manual is proposed as a guidance document for stakeholders during the conduct of audit.
The salient features of the Draft DRM Audit Manual include:
A dedicated clause-wise procedure to verify compliance with Schedule X, covering DRM requirements for SMS, conditional access/encryption, fingerprinting, and STB/software applications.
Scope of work, documentary requirements and audit procedures for pre-signal/compliance audit and the annual Subscription audit.
Prescribed timelines for completion of audits.
Clearly defined roles and responsibilities of the Distribution Platform Operator (DPO), the Broadcaster and the Auditor during the audit process; and
Standard formats for vendor declarations, audit forms and audit reports.
The Draft Telecommunication (Broadcasting and Cable) Services DRM-based Digital Addressable Systems Audit Manual, 2026 has been placed on TRAI's website (www.trai.gov.in).
Written inputs, comments and suggestions if any, supported by detailed reasons, justification and relevant data/evidence are invited from the stakeholders by 30.10.2026. NCEL, NCOL and BBSSL creating new opportunities for grassroots cooperatives through produce aggregation, improved market access and remunerative prices

date:

                09 OCT 2026 3:34PM by PIB Delhi
content:
In furtherance of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi’s vision of ‘Sahkar se Samriddhi’ and under the leadership of Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Shri Amit Shah, the Ministry of Cooperation is working towards transforming India's cooperative sector into a stronger, more inclusive, transparent and economically vibrant ecosystem. As part of these efforts, the two-day 9th National Review Workshop, organised by the Ministry of Cooperation on 8–9 October 2026 in Bastar, Chhattisgarh, under the theme
‘Sahkar se Samriddhi — The Road Ahead: Scaling Impact through Cooperative Transformation’
, concluded today with a renewed emphasis on translating successful cooperative initiatives into practical, time-bound and measurable outcomes at the grassroots level.
The Workshop brought together senior officials from various States, Registrars of Cooperative Societies, representatives of national cooperative institutions and federations, and key stakeholders from across the cooperative sector. Over two days, participants reviewed progress under major initiatives of the Ministry, exchanged successful State-level experiences and discussed strategies for strengthening Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS), cooperative banking, dairy cooperatives, digitalisation, business diversification, cooperative marketing and decentralised grain storage. The deliberations also focused on cooperative development in the North Eastern States and eastern frontier regions, including Left Wing Extremism-affected districts of Chhattisgarh and Odisha.
Delivering the concluding remarks, Secretary, Ministry of Cooperation, Dr. Ashish Kumar Bhutani described the deliberations as highly engaging and productive, noting that the workshop had brought forward a wide range of innovative, practical and district-specific initiatives. He said that one of the most important takeaways was the recognition that no single model of cooperative development could be uniformly applied across the country. Each State has its own circumstances, challenges, traditions and institutional requirements, making locally adapted solutions essential for achieving meaningful results. He emphasised that several successful practices presented during the Workshop were worthy of replication and expansion, and that States should draw upon these experiences while developing their own strategies.
Calling for a stronger focus on implementation, Dr. Bhutani urged States to prepare prioritised action plans immediately after the workshop, clearly identify the officials and institutions responsible for implementation, establish realistic timelines and put in place regular monitoring mechanisms. He said that such an approach would help convert the discussions and recommendations emerging from the Workshop into tangible improvements in the functioning and performance of cooperative institutions. He also observed that some of the most valuable innovations had come from smaller States, demonstrating that larger States could benefit considerably from adopting successful practices developed elsewhere.
Highlighting the presentations made on the functioning of National Cooperative Exports Limited (NCEL), National Cooperative Organics Limited (NCOL) and Bharatiya Beej Sahakari Samiti Limited (BBSSL), the Secretary said that several States had effectively leveraged these national cooperative institutions to strengthen grassroots cooperatives. He noted that these institutions were creating important opportunities for aggregation of agricultural produce, access to wider markets and securing remunerative prices for farmers and cooperative members. Referring to the Ministry's sustained efforts over the past two years to strengthen such linkages, he encouraged other States to study and adopt the successful models presented during the workshop.
Dr. Bhutani also appreciated the deliberations on fertiliser business plans and encouraged States to explore ways of expanding the role of PACS in this sector, wherever feasible. He underlined the importance of developing viable business opportunities for primary cooperative institutions so that they could diversify their activities, strengthen their financial sustainability and provide additional services to their members.
Referring to the cooperative banking session, the Secretary appreciated the innovative initiatives undertaken by several States and said that the Ministry had been working closely with the Ministry of Finance and the Reserve Bank of India to address challenges faced by cooperative banks. He highlighted the importance of strengthening cybersecurity, noting that incidents of cyber fraud in the cooperative banking sector had reinforced the need for robust digital safeguards and greater technological preparedness. He said that cooperative banks must equip themselves with secure and modern banking infrastructure to maintain public confidence and compete effectively with other banking institutions.
Appreciating NABARD's presentation on the development of a robust and uniform Core Banking Solution (CBS) platform, Dr. Bhutani said that the initiative would help address challenges arising from fragmented and unreliable technology systems currently used by some cooperative banks. He noted that the process of establishing the platform was progressing, with the tendering process nearing completion. Access to a modern and standardised banking platform would enable cooperative banks to offer services comparable to those provided by other banks. He emphasised that, alongside cybersecurity, the expansion of internet banking and mobile banking would be critical for improving service delivery, retaining existing customers and attracting younger customers, particularly Generation Z. He also appreciated initiatives undertaken by some cooperative banks to engage this emerging customer segment.
Highlighting the discussions on dairy cooperatives, milk pooling points and milk collection centres, the Secretary reiterated the need to bring informal village-level milk collection arrangements into the organised cooperative framework. He said that village-level systems through which milk is collected for organisations such as Mother Dairy and Amul should be encouraged to develop into formal cooperative institutions, enabling milk producers to benefit from the advantages of cooperative organisation. He noted that dairy and fisheries cooperatives had made encouraging progress in the formation of new societies and stressed the need to build on these achievements.
Turning to the expansion of PACS, Dr. Bhutani acknowledged the challenges faced by States in establishing new primary agricultural credit societies but urged them to accelerate implementation. He referred to the target of establishing approximately 95,000 such institutions over the next two to three years and emphasised the need for focused efforts towards the bifurcation of existing PACS, formation of new societies and expansion of membership. Referring to NABARD's study on the appropriate population coverage for a PACS, he said that increasing membership and creating additional PACS would help build a stronger institutional foundation for cooperative credit delivery. He further observed that a sufficiently broad network of PACS and members was essential for the viability of new District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs).
The Secretary appreciated the successful practices shared by States and Union Territories, including Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, Gujarat, Bihar and Puducherry. He said that these experiences demonstrated how States were identifying their respective strengths and developing cooperative models suited to local needs. Such initiatives could serve as useful templates for other States. He indicated that the proceedings and minutes of the Workshop would identify relevant and adaptable models that States could consider for implementation.
Reviewing progress under PACS computerisation, Dr. Bhutani said that the scheme remained a major centrally funded initiative of the Ministry and urged States to ensure timely completion of pending activities. He informed participants that the existing scheme was scheduled to conclude in March 2027 and that a proposal for its extension without additional financial implications had been sought to facilitate completion of ongoing targets. He stressed that all components of the first phase of PACS computerisation should be completed by December 2026, while audits for the financial years 2024–25 and 2025–26 should be completed by October 2026. He also highlighted the importance of timely reconciliation of accounts and regular updating of records to avoid delays in implementation, particularly during the initial months of the financial year.
Referring to the World's Largest Grain Storage Plan in the cooperative sector, the Secretary said that considerable progress had been made in addressing the initial challenges associated with the initiative. Several States had taken steps towards identifying locations for godowns, securing loan sanctions and initiating construction. He emphasised that these efforts needed to be accelerated and expanded significantly to create a comprehensive ecosystem of decentralised grain storage infrastructure across the country.
Dr. Bhutani also highlighted the potential of decentralised storage infrastructure in developing alternative agricultural marketing and financing arrangements that could help farmers secure remunerative prices for their produce. Referring to recent discussions with the Department of Economic Affairs, he said that the Ministry was exploring alternative models, including pledge finance, which would require a strong network of appropriately developed storage facilities. He clarified that the objective was not to replace the Minimum Support Price (MSP) framework, but to examine additional, sustainable and locally adapted mechanisms for agricultural commodities, particularly cereals other than wheat and paddy, where access to MSP-based procurement could present challenges.
The Secretary said that the Ministry intended to share such models with States over the next two to three months and explore the possibility of implementing pilot projects in selected districts before considering their wider national rollout. He encouraged States to examine these opportunities and contribute practical suggestions for developing farmer-centric models that could improve price realisation, strengthen local agricultural markets and enhance the economic viability of cooperative institutions.
In his concluding remarks, Dr. Bhutani thanked the Chief Secretary of Chhattisgarh, the Government of Chhattisgarh, the Collector of Bastar and the district administration for their support and arrangements for the smooth conduct of the Workshop. He also expressed appreciation for the active participation of representatives from various States and cooperative institutions, observing that the discussions had provided valuable insights for strengthening the cooperative movement. He informed participants that the next National Review Workshop was proposed to be held in Mahabalipuram, Tamil Nadu in January 2027.

A total of 15 Champion Awards were presented at the event, recognising organisations for their achievements in indigenous technology development, product innovation, design, import substitution, manufacturing excellence and exports. RM congratulated the awardees for their contributions to indigenous defence manufacturing, technological innovation, design capabilities, import substitution, manufacturing excellence and exports.
Underlining the importance of the session's theme, “Sovereign Capabilities, Contested Frontiers: Accelerating India's Strategic Autonomy in an Era of Disruption,
”

date:

                09 OCT 2026 7:13PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Mangrol, the
third
Anti-Submarine Warfare Shallow Water Craft (ASW-SWC)
built by Cochin Shipyard Limited (CSL), Kochi,
is set to be commissioned into the Indian Navy on
12 Oct 2026 at Naval Dockyard, Mumbai.
The ceremony will be presided over by VAdm Sanjay Vatsayan, Flag Officer Commanding-in-Chief, Western Naval Command. The event will be attended by senior naval and defence officials, representatives from the Ministry of Defence and Cochin Shipyard Limited, veterans and representatives of indigenous weapons and sensor manufacturers.
Named after Mangrol, a coastal town and prominent fishing harbour in Gujarat's Junagadh district,
the ship carries forward the legacy of the erstwhile INS Mangrol (M85), a minesweeper that served the Indian Navy until 07 Apr 2004. The naming of the ship continues the Navy's tradition of preserving the legacy of its former warships.
Built with over 80% indigenous content,
Mangrol
reflects India's growing capabilities in warship design, construction and integration of advanced weapons and sensors. Constructed by CSL under the Government of India’s
Make in India and
Aatmanirbhar Bharat
initiatives, the ship marks another important step towards self-reliance in defence shipbuilding.
Designed to detect and counter underwater threats in coastal and shallow waters,
Mangrol
is equipped with modern weapons and sensors, including the
Abhay Hull-Mounted Sonar, lightweight torpedoes, an indigenous anti-submarine rocket launcher and the Maareech Advanced Torpedo Decoy System.
Powered by three diesel engines with waterjet propulsion, the ship offers high manoeuvrability for operations in shallow waters. It is also capable of undertaking underwater surveillance, Low-Intensity Maritime Operations and mine warfare-related tasks.
Mangrol will strengthen the Indian Navy's anti-submarine warfare capabilities, particularly in coastal waters where larger warships face operational limitations. The ship can operate alongside maritime patrol aircraft, helicopters and other warships to detect and counter submarine threats. Its induction will enhance the Navy's ability to protect ports, harbours and coastal approaches while supporting wider fleet operations.
Amid growing underwater threats in the evolving maritime security environment, the commissioning of
Mangrol
marks an important milestone in strengthening the Indian Navy's anti-submarine warfare capabilities, particularly in coastal waters. The ship's induction also reflects India's growing indigenous shipbuilding capabilities and reinforces the Navy's commitment to operational preparedness and
Aatmanirbhar Bharat.
